why: Default ASCII load (no optional speedups) parses every facet in Python and pops lines off the front of each 4 KiB chunk. A 20k-triangle scan takes ~154 ms; a single buffer pass should beat 20% and return the same vertices. The 8% spread is well under that, because the loop is interpreter-bound.

Default ASCII save formats and writes seven lines per triangle from Python. The same 20k-triangle patch takes ~141 ms with a 1.9% spread. One byte buffer, still using {:.9g} so the text stays lossless, should beat 20%.

Binary PLY has no speedups path: each vertex is struct.unpack_from and each face is two read calls. A 51k-triangle scanner-style file takes ~114 ms with a 3.6% spread. A dtype view of the common float xyz / list-uchar-int layout should beat 20% with the same vertices and indices.

Each face projects every vertex with its own matmul, so a convex mesh cannot return early. A 1,728-triangle box takes ~100 ms with a 4.0% spread and the cost is quadratic. One batched plane test should beat 20% and return the same boolean.
